topic_summary: Analysis of the Hebrew language revival (1880s-1948) as a contested kernel where 'Hebrew is a living language' was read under fundamentally incompatible interpretive frameworks: a liturgical-preservation reading (recitation of sacred texts constitutes linguistic life) versus a native-generational reading (only daily vernacular transmission constitutes linguistic life). The contest centers on whether symbolic preservation counts as occupying the language-life kernel or whether biological transmission is definitional.

key_entities: Orthodox rabbinical authorities (opponents of secular Hebrew use)
Va'ad Ha-Lashon / Hebrew Language Academy (standardization body, founded 1890)
Jewish immigrant communities (Yemenite, Moroccan, Russian, Kurdish, Bukharan, European waves 1880s-1930s)
Ottoman authorities (political opposition to nationalist language project)
First Hebrew-speaking schools (educational transmission mechanism, late 19th c.)
key_tensions: Sacred vs. secular language use (rabbinical excommunication vs. Ben-Yehuda's daily-use advocacy)
Liturgical preservation vs. native transmission (recitation-as-life vs. mother-tongue-as-life)
Linguistic diversity vs. monolingual nationalism (Yiddish/Ladino/Arabic speakers vs. Hebrew-only policy)
Religious authority vs. secular nationalist authority (who controls Hebrew's legitimate use)
key_mechanisms: Three-pronged revival strategy: Hebrew in Home (first native speaker 1882), Hebrew in School (curriculum replacement), Words-Words-Words (neologism coinage for modern concepts)
Excommunication enforcement (rabbinical sanction against secular Hebrew users)
Lexical expansion via committee (Va'ad Ha-Lashon filling vocabulary gaps for electricity, trains, ice cream)
key_absences: No discussion of whether liturgical Hebrew transmission involved native speakers (children learning prayers) or only adult recitation
No analysis of whether the 'dormancy' claim itself reflects the native-generational reading's interpretive dominance

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The commitment 'Hebrew is a living language' — a shared substrate both parties claim to occupy but read through incompatible frameworks of what constitutes linguistic life
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Rabbinical authority grounds legitimacy in unbroken liturgical transmission from Sinai; Zionist-nationalist authority grounds legitimacy in biological mother-tongue transmission and territorial sovereignty
commitment_system_recognition.candidate_pattern: Interpretive Schism (Pattern 2) — two authority structures claiming the same kernel through mutually exclusive readings, with no institutional mechanism for reconciliation

readings.commitment: A language is alive when its sacred texts are continuously recited, studied, and transmitted in unbroken chain regardless of vernacular use
readings.authority_grounding: Rabbinical tradition: linguistic life = preservation of divine revelation through ritual performance
readings.expected_structural_delta: Hebrew never died (no revival needed); Ben-Yehuda's project is desecration not resurrection; victim set = sacred tradition itself

readings.commitment: A language is alive only when children acquire it as mother tongue and use it for all daily functions including secular mundane speech
readings.authority_grounding: Zionist-nationalist framework: linguistic life = biological transmission + territorial vernacular sovereignty
readings.expected_structural_delta: Hebrew was dead 70-1880 CE (dormancy period real); revival required; victim set = linguistic diversity (Yiddish/Ladino speakers coerced into abandonment)

readings.commitment: A language is alive when it functions as inter-communal medium for practical coordination regardless of native speaker status or sacred function
readings.authority_grounding: Pragmatic-functionalist: linguistic life = communicative utility in multi-lingual contact zones
readings.expected_structural_delta: Hebrew was continuously alive in Jerusalem markets pre-1880 as modified Medieval Hebrew pidgin; neither pure preservation nor pure revival but continuous adaptation

axiom_contradictions.basis: No single coherent framework can hold both 'ritual recitation constitutes linguistic life' and 'only mother-tongue transmission constitutes linguistic life' — accepting one axiom requires rejecting the other as definitionally false

Functionalist framework (life = utility) and nativist framework (life = biological transmission) are mutually exclusive — a pidgin with no native speakers is alive under one axiom, dead under the other

omegas.description: Is the 'dormancy period' (70-1880 CE) itself a product of the native_generational_reading's interpretive dominance? If liturgical_preservation_reading is valid, there was no dormancy — only a category error by historians adopting nativist axioms.

Did liturgical Hebrew involve native child acquisition (learning prayers as first language) or only adult recitation? If children learned liturgical Hebrew natively, the readings may partially collapse — ritual transmission could satisfy biological transmission criterion.

At what point does a pidgin become a native language? If marketplace Hebrew had second-generation speakers using it as primary home language, marketplace_pidgin_reading and native_generational_reading may not be structurally distinct.
omegas.source: Independence Testing (§3.1) — potential Type A overlap
